blocks: Quantum Dot Infrared Photodetectors grown by low pressure metalorganic chemical vapor deposition

We report the fabrication and testing of InGaAs/InGaP quantum dot infrared photodetectors (QDIPs). Self-assembled InGaAs quantum dots were grown on an InGaP matrix using low pressure metalorganic vapor deposition (LP MOCVD). The dot size and uniformity, as well as material quality were optimized by changing the temperature, flow rate, and growth rates throughout the device. Both a high detectivity of 3.6×10¹⁰cm Hz¹ᐟ²/W and low dark current were observed. In addition, a photoresponse with a peak wavelength of 4.7 μm was observed above 200K, varying slightly with changes in temperature. These measurements correlate well with previously predicted advantages of quantum dot photdetector technology over quantum well photodetectors.

Quantum dot (QD) photodetectors have received significant attention within solid-state research due to their potential advantages over quantum well (QW) photodetectors.¹⁻³ QW photodetectors have carriers confined in only one dimension. For example, if the carriers are confined in the z-direction, then they are free to move within the x-y plane. As temperature rises, the energy levels utilized for intersubband transitions are broadened due to the free electron movement within the x-y plane. This, in turn, broadens the detector’s response curve, meaning there is less photocurrent for the detector’s response at a specific wavelength. Due to this chain of events, QW photodetectors must be cooled to increase the photocurrent, increasing their cost and size. In addition, the lack of confinement in the x-y plane means that a QW photodetector cannot respond to normal incident light due to the polarization characteristics of light.

In contrast, quantum dots allow for the three-dimensional confinement of carriers. As a result, a photodetector with quantum dots should not be sensitive to the polarization of incoming light (Fig.1). This feature should reduce the cost and complexity relative to QW photodetectors, which must use Bragg gratings to improve their ability to capture normal incident light waves.

In addition, quantum dots have a Dirac-delta function like density of states at specific energies, allowing very precise wavelength selectivity (Fig. 2). This characteristic could be utilized to construct a multicolor QD photodetector if different sized dots are used within the same photodetector. Phonon scattering rates are also reduced inside quantum dots. The scattering rate between two energy levels is proportional to the overlap of the density of state for those two energy levels⁴ and is also related to the energy difference between the levels. Because the density of states of quantum dots has no overlap between energy levels, the phonon scattering rate is significantly reduced relative to that of quantum wells, provided that the energy difference between the levels is not equal to the phonon energy. This phenomenon is known as “phonon bottleneck,”⁵ and could improve device performance by allowing for a longer carrier lifetime.
